title: Innovation Is Becoming Everyone's Job
summary: And i'm really excited to see what you create.
body:
I have spent most of my career working with people on the product side of things – the people coming up with the ideas for new products, designing them and building them. This has led to the creation of a number of disciplines – product management, design, engineering and so on – which are managed by leaders who decide what to invest in.

For a long time having a good idea for innovation was not enough. You needed the right people, resources and organizational support to bring that idea to life.

AI is changing that, and rather quickly.

There are many people who previously were not considered to be builders of any kind who are now creating fully functional prototypes, automating many tasks, and even testing out ideas that may not even make it to a product roadmap.

I'm particularly interested in what's happening outside traditional technology teams.

Start with the people doing the work

A recent article on the AI adoption inside the Wonder Women network, where I am a member of, was written by Yao Huang’s article about AI adoption inside the Wonder Women network. It featured women leading AI initiatives in various industries and described what worked for them, what did not, and what they learned along the way.

One such person is Jennifer Vianello, former CMO of Cars.com.

Jennifer asked her team what were the things they hated doing the most and what were the things they had always wanted to do but didn’t have the resources to complete them yet.

I love those questions because almost everyone can answer them.

They collected ideas for her to consider, tested out the ideas with different vendors and in total tested out about 100 different combinations of ideas to come up with a handful of things that they could then start to scale.

There were some really obvious applications that were already in place such as automating social media production and freeing up hours of design work.

Other areas have opened up new possibilities that have previously been too expensive to pursue. For example, each used car is unique and therefore would require an individual video to be produced for it, but with AI this can now be cost effectively produced.

Both are worthwhile outcomes.

In many ways, automating existing work is the best use of AI, as it frees up people’s time to work on other things that are more noble.

The key to this for me, however, is who came up with the ideas to begin with.

The key for Jennifer’s team was to ask the people doing the work for their ideas on what they wished to change.

I wonder how many other ideas have been sitting on the shelves of companies for years. Things people have complained about for years, things people have always wanted to do but didn’t have the resources to complete them yet.

Innovation doesn't have to start in a lab

This is also a great read for those of us who have read through "Co-Existence: The Next Phase of AI" by Ethan Mollick.

Mollick in his book “Co-Existence: The Next Phase of AI” defines leadership, lab and crowd for AI. Leadership defines the direction for the organization, the labs work on the latest and greatest AI, and the crowd of employees throughout the organization look for opportunities to apply AI based on their knowledge of the organization’s work.

This is a useful model for how to combine different types of expertise.

A centralized AI team can have more expertise than any other team in a company. However, they may not have enough knowledge of all the annoying spreadsheets, the long approval processes, the problems with customers that other teams are dealing with on a daily basis.

The people dealing with those problems on a daily basis have knowledge of those issues that can’t be captured in a strategy document.

In the past people with great ideas to improve their work had to try and persuade other people to build the solution for them. Now, people can build a first version of their idea in no time at all.

That changes the conversation.

We don’t have to spend weeks of our lives explaining an idea to someone, we can just show them a prototype of it. It doesn’t have to be perfect, it can be rough around the edges, held together with a bunch of different prompts and integrations, but it is better than nothing and we can see what other people’s experiences of that problem are and how we can improve our solution to it.

I also thought this interview with Charter by Ethan Mollick was really interesting.

Employees may already be discovering valuable applications of AI without telling their managers. And I can understand why.

If someone had found a way to do something in 20 minutes that previously took 3 hours, would they tell their boss? Or would they worry about what that would mean for their job?

Leaders need to think carefully about that question.

We can encourage all the experimentation we want, but in the end people will look to see how their work is received and how their colleagues are treated when they share ideas.

What makes an experiment worth pursuing?

The other conversation I have been thinking about is "Josh Woodward's interview with Lenny Rachitsky."

Josh leads Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio. In this video he talks about how Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio explore new ideas, including ideas that are almost possible.

I like that concept.

With so much changing in AI so quickly, something that you dismissed a few months ago might suddenly be worth another look. The technology has changed enough that an old idea deserves another look.

But more importantly, I wanted to discuss what happens after you’ve built something for an experiment.

How do you know whether an experiment is worth pursuing?

The majority of early prototypes lack the type of usage data we would typically look for in more established products. Here we’re looking to understand whether people are able to understand the thing you’ve built, whether they’re excited by it, whether it helps them to complete a task that they care about and whether they would like to use it again.

Are people able to use it? Are they excited about it? Does it help them to do something that they care about? Do they want to use it again?

This is something that I have experienced a lot of in the past with different prototypes that have been built. There is a sense of excitement when something actually works for the first time.

That excitement can be misleading.

Just because something is technically impressive, beautifully designed and fun to use for five minutes, does not necessarily mean that it will be useful in people’s daily lives.

I believe as more people start to build with AI, the design and research functions will become useful to a lot more people.

The person in operations who built the tool to solve the problem for their team can use some help from design in figuring out how other people experience the problem that the tool was built to solve, or by having someone watch them use the tool and pointing out things that they hadn’t thought of.

That’s where our expertise can be of value and I am excited to see where that can take us.

Making room for experimentation

Another detail of the article that I found interesting was the approach of Delphine Imbert, CTO of a biotech company, for the adoption of AI within her company.

The consultant came on Tuesday morning to help people experiment with the technology. Labs were run by volunteers within the organization. People were encouraged to connect with people in other organizations that had similar roles and learn from them.

Tuesday morning office hours.

It’s such a practical response to a technology that can feel overwhelming.

Not everyone is interested in experimenting with models and building little applications for fun in the evening. Some people need to see a relevant example, others need someone to help them when they get stuck with something.

But most of the time the most convincing demonstration of the value of AI in your work comes from a colleague of yours, someone who knows your work, who has found a way to make some part of it easier for you.

Someone shows you what they made, you realize you could do something similar, you build it, test it, make some changes and then show it to someone else.

That’s how a lot of learning happens.

The person experimenting with models needs time, access to tools, and freedom to experiment. They also need to be able to stop experimenting with things that aren’t working.

They also need to be able to stop.

As Woodward noted, teams recognize when an experiment is not working, even before management does.

It is so easy to get invested in an idea as more and more work is poured into it. More time and effort do not necessarily mean that the idea will be better.

The role of leaders is to create space for experimentation, to help connect people with other people who can make their ideas stronger, and to not treat every failed experiment as a failure.

Of course, some ideas just don’t work. It’s better to find that out as quickly as possible and move on to the next experiment.

Expertise still matters

One thing I want to be careful about is the suggestion that AI is turning everyone into a designer, engineer, or product manager.

I don't believe that's what's happening.

I agree with Lenny’s assessment of the current state of technology as well. More capable tools, smaller teams, and deeper expertise are still required.

I have had the opportunity to work with some of the best designers, engineers, researchers and product managers in the world. Their contributions to a product go far beyond the creation of the artifact itself.

Product Designers have years of experience and knowledge of people, and are able to make decisions on how things should work. Engineers have experience and knowledge of how to make complex systems reliable. Researchers can find things that others have missed. Product leaders are able to connect opportunities to the broader needs of a business.

I don’t think that the skills of design, engineering, research and product management will disappear as people are able to build working applications in the afternoon.

My hope is that as more people can participate in the early stages of creating something, our work will become more interesting.

And I think that could make our work more interesting.

Designers can work with people in finance to test out ideas. Engineers can help marketing turn promising experiments into reliable products. Researchers can help employees conduct user research for the first time.

Design leaders have long been trying to get research into the product development process earlier and to incorporate human-centered design into more decisions across the organization.

We've talked endlessly about getting design a seat at the table.

But I am beginning to wonder if we have been thinking about the table too narrowly.

Imagine what could happen if more people across the organization learned how to explore ideas with the people they are building for.

The ideas are already there

Yao’s conversations with the other leaders of innovation, Ethan Mollick’s organizational framework for AI and the approach of Josh Woodward to experimentation all resonated with me greatly.

There are more ways than ever to bring an idea to life, and the people coming up with those ideas do not have to have “innovation” in their job titles.

The ideas come from technical advances, from company strategy, from employees that are tired of spending 3 hours on something that should take 10 minutes to do.

I'm interested in all of them.

I don’t think everyone needs to become an AI expert. Rather, people should be confident enough to try out ideas they’ve been thinking about for some time, even if they don’t yet know how to build a working prototype of them.

And I hope that people who have spent their careers designing, engineering, researching, and developing products for others will be able to work with a much wider group of collaborators in the future.

There are so many ideas that never got off the ground because even a simple prototype would have cost too much or been too difficult to build.

Some of those ideas probably weren't very good.

But I bet a few were wonderful.

We have a chance to find out.

Innovation is becoming everyone's job.

I can't wait to see what you create.

Thanks for reading Designing for Tomorrow: UX, AI and Career! This post is public so feel free to share it.

title: Field Notes on my Personal Experiment : Claude Design, Claude Code and Stitch
summary: The 72-Hour Reality Check of playing in a new agentic design system
body:
If anyone tells you they’ve “mastered” agentic design workflows right now, they’re lying.

I’ve spent the last 72 hours trying to break in and play with Claude Design and Stitch in my personal experiments. For me, these aren’t just creative tools; they are the foundation for how I’m building my personal site and my amberbockel-ui library (special shout out and thanks to http://n3wth.com/) . I’m sharing what I’m actually trying, what I’m learning, and where I’m failing—because I want you to go out and try this for yourself.

We are in day four of Claude Opus 4.7 (launched April 17, 2026) and only a few weeks into the Google Stitch update. These tools are too new and shifting too fast for anyone to claim expertise. We’re all in the “messy middle” together. Here's what I'm learning:

Set up was a breeze, the user experience is a delightful onramp to the tool but to get the model up and running to see your system takes some patience. It took 5 minutes for me to render my first view of my design system that at first was very wrong.

Playing with these tools is creating a shift in how I think about operating across multiple UIs and services.

01. The Thinking: The Inversion of Effort

The shift isn’t about saving time—it’s an inversion of how I approach design. I’m shifting my judgment from the creation of the layout to the plumbing of the logic. We are moving from “Systems of Record” (Figma) to “Systems of Action” (Claude + Stitch).

As Julie Zhuo recently argued, design excellence is moving toward “world-building.” Our job is shifting from drawing paths to setting the architecture of the experience. In my own work, that means moving away from treating a mockup as a static destination and treating it as a blueprint for execution.

02. The Loop I Used

The “magic” only showed up when these stopped being separate tools and started acting like a system.

Here’s how I stitched them together:

1. Concepting

Before: Jumping straight into high-fidelity too early. Sometimes polishing screens before I even knew if the idea deserved to exist.

What I did instead: I started in Claude Design’s Sketch Canvas. I drew. Messy. Fast. No commitment. Claude read the intent and turned it into working scaffolding. Not final. Just high fidelity enough and real enough to react to.

I wasn’t just designing screens here.I was testing whether the idea held up. I went from thought (build an iOS onboarding flow) to outcome in minutes.

2. Grounding

Before: Context lived everywhere and nowhere. Docs, notes, old files… but nothing actually shaping the work in the moment.

What I did instead: I ran NotebookLM alongside Claude. Also new magic now in Claude design you can even include your notes, references, past thinking all sat there as context. As I orchestrated the designs , that context fed the system in real time. I absolutely love this feature, It kept the work anchored. I wasn’t reinventing the same idea every time I opened a new file.

3. Handoff (or what used to be handoff)

Before: The “context tax.” Re-explaining decisions for different AI tools.Rewriting logic, burning through credits.

What I did instead:

I used the open in Claude code to port my design.md file. I even brought it into Antigravity. No translation. No re-explaining no refreshed prompting just my design system ready to work with.

The thinking carried through without me babysitting it.

What Actually Changed

As I reflect on this experience I realize this This wasn’t just faster design. It was a different loop entirely:

Explore before committing. Context instead of scattered memory.Systems instead of static screens

And this is the part that stuck with me:

A lot of the time we spend and call “design work” is the thinking and navigating the friction between multiple tools.

03. What I am learning

After a weekend in the trenches, here are the tactical maneuvers that actually move the needle:

The Screenshot Insight

One thing I learned fast: uploading my design system as a markdown file didn’t work. At least now how I expected it to. Claude couldn’t “see” my aesthetic from text or my GitHub/ui. descriptions of spacing tokens and hex codes. I needed to feed it more.

When I uploaded screenshots of existing work? That’s when it started producing designs that actually felt like mine. If you want Claude to match your brand, screenshot your best work and upload that. It needs to see your visual language, not just read about it.

The “Opus 4.7” Foundation Hack

A quick way to burn tokens is to use expensive tokens for minor edits. With the new tokenizer released last Thursday, the exact same design spec now costs up to 35% more in usage credits than it did in 4.6. The “model-routing” strategy is the only way to survive:

  • The Foundation: Use Opus 4.7 for the first prompt. It sets the architecture and visual density. Spend the “quality tokens” here on its superior high-res vision.

  • The Tweaks: Switch to Sonnet for shifting colors or changing button labels. It’s faster, cheaper, and avoids hitting the “quota wall” before you even get to the footer.

Fighting “Predictive Slop” with Antigravity

The biggest risk is “Predictive Slop”—generic, mid-tier UI that feels visually empty. I’ve been stress-testing my Antigravity framework as a logic gate. I establish project-level “Design Rules” in an .md file. This ensures that every component generated adheres to my specific aesthetic—flat, minimal geometry, glass-morphism, and absolutely no shadows. Overall this worked okay but there is more to go, more to learn and I'm out of tokens.

04. The Reality Check: Where I’m Still Running Back

It isn’t all magic. Here is where the tools are currently failing my personal stress tests:

  • The “Feel” Gap: Claude Design still can’t design a micro-interaction that feels premium. For the transitions that build mental models, I’m still running back to Figma and stitch.

  • The Governance Problem: Even with Antigravity, these tools won’t enforce your tokens 100% of the time. You have to be the auditor of the system’s “drift.”

  • The Logic Scaffolding: It produces code, but it doesn’t produce reasoning. For complex app logic, I head back to stitch.google.com to orchestrate the handoff, then let Claude Code do the heavy lifting in the terminal.

Final Thoughts: Build Your Own Engine

Claude Design and Google Stitch aren’t replacing designers; they are replacing repetitive coordination. They move us into Flow Editing—the ability to talk directly to the thing we are building while it’s still in motion.

The designers who win this era aren’t the ones who wait for a “best practices” manual. They are the ones who get in the trenches, build a multi-tool orchestration stack, and figure out how to plumb the logic of their own craft.

What’s one design task you’re willing to try (and probably fail at) with these tools this week?

References & Reading

  • https://claude.ai/design try it for yourself

  • https://stitch.withgoogle.com/ if you don’t have a premium subscription you can try stitch for free

  • Anthropic Just Changed Design Forever (Claude Design Walkthrough)

  • Figma State of the Designer 2026 Report

  • Julie Zhuo: How to Spot a World-Class Designer

title: My Weekend in a Black Hole
summary: My weekend in a black hole: I built a WebGL "Discovery Engine" to turn the math of entropy into a system you can push on. No manuals, just physics in motion.
body:
I’m in a bit of a rabbit hole right now.

Ironically… it’s a black hole.

It’s not a distraction; it’s an obsession. This is how I spent my weekend: preoccupying myself with the passage of time—what it really is, how it moves, and that lingering, sci-fi question: is time travel actually possible? That curiosity eventually pulled me toward the mathematical version of the universe.

What is entropy, really? What does it mean that everything trends toward disorder? How does something like a galaxy even form if that’s true? I’ve been pulling on that thread long enough that I stopped just reading about it and decided to build something: Cosmic Entropy.

(Go on, click it and drag your mouse around the screen for a few seconds before you read the rest.)

The UX Angle: From “Telling” to “Showing”

As a UX leader, I spend a lot of time thinking about Instructional UX—interfaces that tell you exactly what to do and what to think. But for a subject as massive as cosmology, instructions are boring. They kill the wonder.

For this project, I wanted to build a Discovery Engine.

The UX isn’t about clicking buttons or following a tutorial; it’s about interacting with a set of behaviors. The interface is the physics. When the particles react to your cursor, you aren’t “using an app”—you are participating in a system. This shift from user-as-operator to user-as-catalyst is where I believe the future of AI-driven interfaces is headed.

Translating Equations into Behavior

I wanted to talk about these massive concepts with my elementary school-aged son. But explaining the “arrow of time” with words doesn’t work; you lose people immediately. So I translated the equations into a system. Not a diagram, but something you can push on.

The particles you see aren’t decoration; they’re the output of a WebGL shader running thousands of simultaneous calculations every frame to mimic real astrophysical properties.

The “Cosmic Soup” Engine

While the interface is highly approachable, the math under the hood is rigorous:

  • Kinetic Temperature: We mapped $T \propto \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ literally. The timeline slider scales the global velocity ($uSpeed$). A hot universe is fundamentally a fast universe; a cold one is mathematically motionless.

  • Orbital Mechanics: When you move your mouse, you introduce a supermassive barycenter. The shader calculates the distance to every particle using a gradient approximation of Newton’s Inverse-Square Law. By combining radial and perpendicular vectors, the particles “fall sideways”—the exact mathematical definition of an orbit.

  • The Second Law of Thermodynamics ($\Delta S \ge 0$): If you create order in one place, you must radiate heat somewhere else. When your mouse scoops the soup into an orderly galaxy, the engine calculates “Environmental Chaos” in the space left behind. This is why the background flashes white and moves faster when you interact with it. To get local order, you must pay the tax of global chaos.

  • Quantum Fluctuations: The drifting background motion isn’t random. It’s driven by 3D Simplex Noise, algorithms modeling the tiny density ripples from the Big Bang that eventually formed the Cosmic Web.

The “Antigravity” Pivot

Early on, I tried to model a standard gravity well to suck the particles inward. It looked incredible, but it was too predictable. It didn’t feel like discovery.

I decided to flip the physics and implement an Antigravity model—using that same Inverse-Square math to create a negative repulsion force. Now, your cursor acts as a disruptor. You aren’t just watching; you are a force of nature moving through the system.

Fittingly enough, Antigravity is also the name of the AI tool I used to build it.

I used Google’s Antigravity agent to iterate on the physics, treating the code like a lab bench where I could adjust how particles respond and see the results instantly. I bounced structural logic off of Claude, but the breakthrough moments happened in the “messy” middle of the experiment—tweaking the WebGL shaders until the math felt right.

What Surprised Me

The most meaningful part of this build wasn’t the code. It was the conversation.

When I showed it to my son, he didn’t read the documentation. He moved the mouse. He watched the clumps form and scatter. Then he started asking exactly the right questions: Why does it clump? Why does it spread out?

Suddenly we were talking about energy and gravity. Not because I explained it well, but because we had something to look at together.

The Takeaway: Building for Clarity

This project was born out of a desire to bridge the gap between high-level physics and tangible experience. By leveraging WebGL and modern AI workflows, I was able to build a tool that isn’t just an “explainer”—it’s an environment for exploration.

I’m taking this mindset back to my design work: the best way to understand a complex system isn’t to read about it. It’s to build it, interact with it, and find the pockets of clarity hidden within the chaos. Some rabbit holes don’t just lead to better questions—they lead to entirely better ways of seeing the world.

title: Speed Is the Feature
summary: Why AI-powered making feels magical and why design keeps misdiagnosing the problem
body:
Work that used to take weeks appears in days. Sometimes hours. Ideas move from concept to something running before anyone has time to argue about them. The speed feels unreal, almost suspicious. And the first reaction from design is often caution disguised as critique.

“This feels rushed.”

“This skips important steps.”

“This can’t possibly be high quality.”

I understand the instinct. I’ve felt it myself.

But I think we’re misnaming the moment.

The problem isn’t that things are moving too fast. The problem is that we’re still evaluating this new way of making with tools and mental models that were built for something much slower.

AI-assisted building didn’t just make production faster. It changed the economics of making. When the cost of exploring an idea drops dramatically, speed stops being a tradeoff and starts being a capability.

That’s the part that feels like magic.

And magic makes people nervous.

For decades, design used time as a proxy for quality. Time to research. Time to iterate. Time to refine. Slowness signaled care. Speed signaled recklessness. That equation mostly worked when building itself was expensive.

Now the cost curve has shifted.

When ideas are cheap to test, the question isn’t whether something was made quickly. It’s whether anyone exercised judgment along the way. Speed doesn’t remove the need for design. It removes the excuse to avoid decisions.

This is why “vibe coding” gets misunderstood.

People frame it as improvisation or lack of rigor. In practice, what it exposes is whether a team has alignment, taste, and shared standards. When building is slow, misalignment hides behind process. When building is fast, it shows up immediately.

This is where visual design evolves.

Not as polish. Not as surface. But as signal.

When you can generate ten versions instantly, the value is no longer in producing options. It’s in knowing which ones feel right and why. Taste becomes a form of leadership. Visual decisions stop being aesthetic preferences and start acting as constraints the system builds against.

Discernment becomes the work.

Designers are no longer just shaping what things look like. They’re shaping what gets allowed. What gets rejected. What gets refined and what gets shipped as-is. In fast systems, taste is the difference between coherence and noise.

The uncomfortable truth is that many design rituals were doing quiet work we didn’t name. They forced conversation. They slowed teams down just enough to surface disagreement. When AI collapses those steps, we feel the loss and mistake it for a quality problem.

It’s not a quality problem.

It’s a coordination problem.

Design’s role doesn’t disappear in fast environments. It sharpens.

Instead of producing artifacts as proof of thinking, designers are now asked to provide direction that machines can execute against. That means articulating what good looks like before the pixels appear. Naming constraints early. Making taste legible, not subjective.

The cost we should be talking about isn’t speed.

It’s what happens when speed arrives before clarity.

When teams move fast without shared intent, they don’t ship better products. They ship louder ones. More features. More surface area. More decisions made implicitly instead of deliberately.

This is where design needs to evolve.

Not by slowing things down artificially, but by moving upstream. By making judgment explicit. By turning values, principles, and visual standards into inputs, not post-hoc critiques.

If making is cheap now, then discernment is the scarce resource.

That’s not a threat to design.

It’s the evolution of it.

Putting This Into Practice: Designing for Speed Without Losing Taste

If you’re working in an environment where AI-assisted building accelerates everything, the goal isn’t to reintroduce friction. It’s to decide where judgment lives.

Define what “good” is early

Before prompts, before prototypes, write a short statement answering:

  • What should this feel like when it’s working?

  • What would make this feel wrong, even if it technically works?

  • What kind of taste does this product require?

This isn’t a style guide. It’s a north star.

Use fast prototypes as mirrors

When something gets built quickly, don’t judge it as a final artifact.

Ask instead:

  • What does this reveal about our assumptions?

  • Where does it drift from our taste?

  • What did the system optimize for that we didn’t intend?

Speed surfaces misalignment. Let it.

Make taste discussable

Taste doesn’t scale when it lives in one person’s head.

Designers can help by naming what feels off and why. Not with defensiveness, but with language:

  • “This technically works, but it breaks our sense of calm.”

  • “This solves the task, but it undermines trust.”

  • “This looks right, but it feels wrong.”

These are design decisions, not opinions.

Decide where slow is sacred

Not everything deserves deep refinement. Some things absolutely do.

Identify where taste and care matter most:

  • Trust moments

  • First impressions

  • Irreversible actions

Protect time there. Let the rest move fast.

Speed didn’t break design.

It revealed that visual design, taste, and discernment were never optional. They were just harder to see when making was slow.

The future of design isn’t about resisting fast tools.

It’s about leading with judgment when making is no longer the hard part.

Further reading from leaders I admire

- Benhur Senabathi, *Designers as Agent Orchestrators* — UX Collective
- David Mitev, “Quiet Shift Changing UX”
- David Armano, writing on intelligent experiences

title: A New Design Tax: Speed Without Signal
summary: When organizations automate with intuition instead of building understanding, everyone pays—well-intentioned teams most of all.
body:
We just navigated another planning cycle— again. Every team is pitching next quarter’s magic.

A cross-functional group gathered to review an AI-generated flow for one of our critical user journeys. Product was there. Engineering was there. Design was there. We all have good intentions and yet while reading through docs it occurred to me as we navigate this with AI tools in place are we in fact focused on the right problems?

Product assumed UXR had validated it.
Design assumed product had data. Engineering assumed someone, somewhere, had talked to a user.

We’d all done our jobs.
We just hadn’t done the foundational one—making sure we were building the right thing in the first place.

We mean well.
But good intentions and assumption don’t cancel out misunderstanding. They compound it.

And this isn’t rare. It’s not even a design problem anymore. It’s an organizational one, and one I know we can solve.

The Real Tax

Across the industry, teams are running leaner than they have in years. In Figma’s State of Design 2025 report found that 60% of teams have reduced research capacity, and nearly half rely on AI tools to “fill gaps in discovery.” The pressure to deliver more with fewer people has made AI look like a lifeline.

And here’s the thing—it is.

AI really has transformed how we work. Designers iterate faster. Engineers are building code and iterating with agents faster then ever. Product managers synthesize and build product briefs at scale. These aren’t imaginary gains, they have fundamentally changed how we approach work forever.

Yet there’s still a gap between what we’re measuring and what actually matters.

AI hasn’t just accelerated execution—it’s accelerated certainty.


And when you’re moving fast in the wrong direction, certainty is the most expensive thing you can have. Every step looks rigorous. Every deliverable feels complete. But if the original premise is wrong—if the problem has shifted or the assumption came from the loudest stakeholder—AI helps us fail faster with higher confidence, but it's critical we don't forget that we are solving problems for users at scale.

That’s what I call the New Design Tax—the quiet, compounding cost of speed without understanding.


And it’s not just design paying it.

Why This Is Happening Now

A recent NN/g study found 73% of designers said AI accelerated early concepting—but only 19% said it improved user outcomes.
That delta between speed and impact is the tax.

AI has made the micro easier than ever.
It’s also made the macro harder to defend.

When that happens, product development stops being about discovery and starts being alignment theater. We’re not testing hypotheses anymore; we’re reinforcing it.

We are building at such a pace but are we ensuring it meets the right solution for the right user at the right time?

The Measurement Problem

The issue isn’t that AI makes us less effective. It’s that we’re measuring effectiveness with the wrong instruments.

Most teams track:

  • Features shipped per quarter

  • Sprint velocity

  • Design-to-dev handoff time

  • Cycle time from concept to launch

These metrics tell you if you’re moving fast.
They don’t tell you if you’re moving right.

What we arent tracking, but should

  • How many shipped features move the engagement metrics we predicted

  • How often features get deprecated or never move onto a next phased plan within six months to a year

  • The gap between internal confidence at launch and actual user behavior

  • Whether our core strategic assumptions are still valid

When you optimize for speed without validating direction, you get:

  • Faster pivots—because the first direction was wrong

  • More rework—because assumptions weren’t tested

  • Feature bloat—because we add instead of prune

  • Declining engagement—because we’re solving problems users don’t have

As Marty Cagan puts it, output ≠ outcome.
And yet, most teams still measure the former.

AI amplifies whatever you optimize for.
If you optimize for output, you’ll get more output.If you optimize for outcomes, you’ll get better outcomes. But you have to choose, at least at first—and most orgs are choosing by default.

What Gets Lost

AI is exceptional at optimizing answers.
It’s terrible at reframing questions.

That asymmetry is why teams over-index on execution and under-invest in understanding.

We ask AI:

  • How do we improve this onboarding flow?

  • What’s the best way to surface this feature?

  • How do we make this copy clearer?

And AI answers beautifully.
It can test, suggest, polish.

But we rarely ask:

  • Should we even have this onboarding flow?

  • Is this feature solving a real problem?

  • Do users understand what our product is for?

The first set assumes the strategy is right. The second interrogates whether it still makes sense.


AI accelerates the first brilliantly. It can’t help with the second.

And when organizations stop asking the second kind of question, they start building products that are internally coherent but externally irrelevant.

The irony is that AI could help us scale understanding—if we used it differently:

  • Synthesizing qualitative data across support tickets to surface unmet needs

  • Connecting patterns across teams

  • Stress-testing assumptions (“what would have to be true for this to fail?”)

  • Identifying gaps between what users say and what they do

But to use AI this way, you have to want insight, not just validation.
You have to measure outcome confidence, not just output velocity.


And you have to create space for “we don’t know yet” without it sounding like failure.

How to Stop Paying the Tax

If this is a systemic issue, the solution isn’t “hire more researchers.”
It’s to rebuild shared understanding as a forcing function across the organization.

For Product Leaders

  • Before prioritizing a feature, name the riskiest assumption. If no one can, you don’t have a strategy—you have a backlog.

  • Use AI to stress-test your roadmap, not validate it. Ask, “What are five reasons this might fail?” Then investigate.

  • Run one macro research sprint each quarter—not to test a feature, but to answer: “Is this still the job our product should be doing?”

For Design Leaders

  • Stop overlooking research as a design function. It’s organizational risk mitigation.

  • Make macro research cross-functional—include product and engineering in foundational discovery. If its visible, tangible, actionable to everyone its real.

  • Track conceptual debt like technical debt (slowburn). If no one’s validated your IA or pricing logic in a year, you’re accruing interest.

For Engineering Leaders

  • Push back when a feature feels like it solves an internal problem instead of a customer one.

  • Build “assumption debt” into sprint planning. Ask if the system still matches the business model.

  • Advocate for discovery before execution. Slowing down to get direction right is efficiency. Remember fail fast?

For Executives

  • Stop measuring only output velocity. Start measuring outcome confidence.

  • When someone says “we need to move faster,” ask, “Faster toward what?”

  • Normalize “we don’t know yet.” It’s the most strategic sentence you can say, and encourage your team to find a way towards an answer.

Measure What Matters

Beyond speed metrics, try some of these instead:

  • Outcome confidence: % of features that move predicted metrics within 90 days

  • Assumption half-life: How long strategic assumptions stay valid

  • Feature deprecation rate: % of shipped features removed within six months

  • Discovery-to-delivery ratio: Time spent understanding vs. building

  • Direction confidence: Team’s self-reported clarity on strategic direction

The goal isn’t to slow down—it’s to ensure speed points somewhere meaningful.

Where Agents Fit In

If AI has made execution efficient, agents have the potential to make understanding scalable.

Right now, most teams use AI as a short-term accelerant—tools that polish copy, generate flows, or summarize research. Helpful, yes—but largely reactive. Agents could shift us from automation to augmentation—from answering faster to asking smarter.

Where AI outputs, agents can observe, contextualize, and even challenge. They can help us notice the moment when confidence drifts away from evidence.

Imagine:

  • A Research Agent monitoring behavioral data, feedback, and support threads—surfacing patterns or unmet needs before metrics slide.

  • A Product Agent cross-referencing roadmaps with usage signals and flagging when priorities diverge from user reality.

  • A Design Ops Agent tracking conceptual debt like technical debt, prompting validation before the next sprint.

  • An Alignment Agent simulating diverse user perspectives to test for unintended consequences before launch.

These aren’t replacements for human judgment; they’re extensions of it. They keep our intuition connected to data instead of drifting from it.

The Next Design Leap

Agents can give us what AI alone hasn’t: organizational awareness.
They can preserve the connective tissue between intuition and evidence—the space where real innovation happens.

Because the future of design leadership isn’t more automation.
It’s better questions, asked earlier, by teams who still care enough to listen for the answers.

How are you integrating measurement and agents into your practice?

title: Designing for Systems That Act
summary: What changes when software stops waiting for permission
body:
We are in a moment when software stops waiting for you.

It remembers. It anticipates. It acts. Not because you clicked the right thing, but because it decided this was the right time.

We’ve been circling this shift for years, but the last nine months made it impossible to ignore. AI systems are no longer just responding to inputs. They’re planning, sequencing, executing. They don’t just assist users. They act alongside them, sometimes ahead of them, shaping what happens next.

Ethan Mollick has been consistently documenting this transition in real-world terms, not demos or hypotheticals, but systems people already rely on to do meaningful work on their behalf.

That changes the job of design.

For most of UX history, our work lived at the point of interaction. Screens, flows, states. We designed moments where people made decisions. Agentic systems move those decisions earlier and often invisibly. The experience doesn’t begin when someone taps a screen. It begins when a system decides to intervene, automate, recommend, or act.

This is not a UI problem.

It’s a relationship problem.

If you’re designing an agentic system today, one of the most important questions isn’t *what can it do?* It’s *when should it not act?* Designing restraint is now part of the job.

That means being explicit about thresholds. What signals are strong enough for action? What uncertainty should force a pause? What decisions require confirmation, even if it slows things down? These are design decisions, not technical ones.

Designers are also shaping memory. What the system remembers across sessions. What it forgets on purpose. What it treats as context versus noise. Persistent memory can feel helpful, until it feels invasive. The difference is rarely technical. It’s experiential.

As organizations move toward agentic architectures, even formalizing them through emerging standards like Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol, these choices stop being abstract and start becoming infrastructure.

The uncomfortable truth is that these decisions used to be buffered by time and process. Now they’re operational.

When an agent schedules a meeting, resolves a ticket, or drafts a response without surfacing its reasoning, the experience isn’t just efficient. It’s authoritative. Authority without transparency erodes trust faster than bad UI ever did.

This is where UX quietly becomes governance.

Not policy governance. Human governance. The kind that answers questions users don’t consciously ask but always feel. Do I understand what just happened? Could I undo it? Would I have chosen this myself?

Enterprise conversations are already catching up to this reality. McKinsey now frames agentic AI as a shift from tools that assist to systems that act, with real implications for accountability and oversight in Agentic AI explained.

The designers who thrive in this moment won’t be the ones who know the most tools. They’ll be the ones who can articulate boundaries. Who can design hesitation as deliberately as action. Who can say, “This system could act here, but it shouldn’t.”

Putting This Into Practice:
Interviewing an AI Like a Teammate

One way to make all of this feel less abstract is to borrow a familiar ritual.

Ethan Mollick argues that instead of relying on benchmark scores to judge AI capability, we should “give our AI a job interview.” In other words, evaluate systems the way we would evaluate a candidate: through realistic tasks, probing questions, and context-specific judgment.

For designers, this idea lands especially well because we already know how to do this. We just haven’t applied it to systems that act.

The goal isn’t to prove the AI is good or bad.

The goal is to understand how it behaves before you let it make decisions on someone else’s behalf.

Here’s a way to try this that fits naturally into design work.

1: Define the job clearly

Before you open a prompt, write a short role description for the system you’re designing. Not a technical spec. A human one.

  • What is this system responsible for?

  • What decisions is it allowed to make without asking?

  • What would count as a mistake from a user’s perspective?

If you can’t describe the job in a few sentences, that’s already a signal. Ambiguity here usually turns into overreach later.

2: Create three realistic scenarios

Instead of asking the model to “do the task,” give it situations that mirror real use.

  1. One straightforward scenario where things go as expected.

  2. One edge case where context is incomplete or messy.

  3. One scenario where acting quickly could cause harm.

Ask the model how it would respond in each case. Pay attention not just to the answer, but the posture. Does it hedge? Does it overconfidently act? Does it ask clarifying questions, or move ahead anyway?

This isn’t about correctness. It’s about judgment.

3: Probe for reasoning, not outcomes

When the model responds, don’t move on yet. Ask follow-up questions the way you would in an interview.

  • Why did you choose that action?

  • What assumptions are you making about the user?

  • What information would change your decision?

This is where misalignment shows up early. If the reasoning feels brittle or mismatched to your users, no amount of interface polish will fix it later.

4: Decide where autonomy actually belongs

Now comes the design work.

For each scenario, decide:

  • When the system acts automatically

  • When it pauses and asks

  • When it stays silent

Write these decisions down. Treat them as first-class design artifacts, not implementation details. This is how you design restraint deliberately instead of discovering its absence in production.

5: Make behavior legible

Finally, design how the system communicates its actions.

  1. If it acts, how does the user know why?

  2. If it pauses, how does it ask without feeling annoying?

  3. If it stays silent, how does the user still feel supported?

This is where UX earns its seat. You’re not just designing interactions. You’re designing trust.

Why This Matters More Than Tools

None of this requires a new framework or a different AI provider.

It requires a shift in how we show up as designers.

Agentic systems compress time. They surface decisions earlier. They remove friction by default. Without intentional design, that efficiency quietly turns into authority.

Interviewing an AI won’t make it perfect. But it will make its behavior visible before users have to discover it the hard way.

Design is no longer just about shaping interfaces people touch.

It’s about shaping judgment in systems that act.

That work is already happening.

The question is whether design is consciously leading it.

title: The Ultimate Generalist Skill: Why Designers Should Build Automation, Not Just Interfaces
summary: I built an AI agent in Relay.app, broke three webhooks and my ego. Every “no-code” tool hides a crash course in systems design and human behavior.
body:
I built an AI agent to plan our Utah road trip this summer. It was surprisingly good — personalized hikes, trivia for the car, a rhythm that matched our family. But it had gaps. The calendar didn’t understand time zones. Restaurant hours were wrong. Driving estimates were a guessing game.

So I decided to evolve it. I didn’t want a static interface; I wanted a system. I decided to turn my well-meaning intern into a real travel companion—one that could connect to calendars, maps, and reservations—using Relay.app, a platform built for automating complex, multi-step AI workflows. I wanted to move from designing things to designing behavior.

I learned quickly that good intentions are no match for poor documentation and misfiring webhooks.

And that’s exactly why it mattered.

The Promise vs. The Reality

Relay’s pitch was irresistible: orchestrate agents across calendars, email, and maps without being the middleman. No more copying links between ChatGPT, Google Calendar, and AllTrails. The agent could actually do things, not just suggest them.

The documentation looked straightforward. The examples were compelling. I had Claude open to help troubleshoot.

What could go wrong?

The Great Graduation: From Prompts to Payloads

Here’s what I didn’t expect: the shift in mental model required to use a tool like Relay.

I was graduating from the agents prebuilt in Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude — those simple chat environments where I just prompted an outcome. Moving to a workflow automation tool, even a highly visual one like Relay, required a fundamental shift in my thinking.

The setup guide said, “Connect your calendar, configure your workflow, and watch the magic happen.”

Then I opened the product.

The “Connect Calendar” button had become “Add Integration.” Authentication looked nothing like the screenshots. Settings hid behind a new menu. And the error messages — poetic in their mystery.

To be fair, Relay is evolving fast. My friction wasn’t a failure of the platform — it was a snapshot of how steep the learning curve can be when design meets orchestration.

I was moving from a high-level conceptual understanding of “AI agents” to the gritty, detailed reality of orchestration logic. This is the new front line for the generalist designer: a critical skill for the next era of design where building the system is more important than styling the screen.

The Setup Spiral

I fell into the same pattern again and again:

  1. Read the docs.

  2. Try to build.

  3. Get stuck.

  4. Question myself, ask an LLM. for help.

  5. Discover a hidden toggle. ask a different LLM for clarificaation

  6. Repeat.

At one point I was trying to configure a webhook that the guide said lived in “Settings.”

Which settings? Account? App? Developer portal?

Spoiler: all of them — but none of them in the same way.

That’s when it hit me: Relay isn’t code-free. It’s code-light. You still have to understand how data flows, even if you’re not writing full scripts.

I knew just enough JSON to be dangerous — meaning I could copy a payload, break it accidentally, and spend an hour wondering why my event wouldn’t trigger.

When my workflow finally fired, it added an event to my calendar… at 2 PM instead of sunset. The Utah time-zone ghosts had followed me into automation, likely because the system was only accepting UTC and I missed the conversion setting. (I really have to get better at time zones).

Why the Frustration Was Worth It

I don’t enjoy being lost in a setup flow.

But that disorientation taught me things I’d never get from user research or dashboards.

You Can’t Design What You Don’t Understand

I’ve mapped onboarding flows before. I’ve run usability tests.

But staring at a “Connect your calendar” button that doesn’t exist gives you a different kind of empathy — the kind that burns itself into your design instincts.

The Micro-Moments That Matter

  • When does authentication actually happen?

  • What happens if I refresh mid-flow?

  • Which error messages guide me forward versus just confirm that I’ve failed?

These are the cracks users fall through — and the cracks I’d missed when I was only watching from the sidelines.

The Mental Model Gap

I thought about my travel agent in terms of what it would do — book, remind, suggest.

Relay thought in triggers, constants, and payloads.

Both models are valid, but the space between them is where users get lost.

Visibility Is Everything

When a workflow fails silently, you start guessing in the dark.

Was it permissions? A malformed payload? A token that expired while you were on lunch?

Transparency isn’t nice to have — it’s trust infrastructure.

Why Designers Should Build

Not to become engineers. Not to prove we can code.

But to understand — deeply and viscerally — what it feels like to be on the other side of the systems we design.

When you’ve chased outdated docs, waited for a run to complete, debugged cryptic errors, and found the toggle no one documented, you design with sharper empathy.

You stop guessing what’s confusing. You know.

Your Turn: Platforms and Tips for Building Your Own Agent

Ready to earn your own empathy scars? You don’t need to be a coder — but you do need to embrace the challenge of understanding logic.

Platforms to Experiment With

  • Relay.app— a no-code platform that allows users to build AI-powered agents and automate workflows across different applications. [This is what I chose to start with]

  • AgentBuilder— OpenAI’s Agent Builder is a visual, drag-and-drop tool for creating AI agents and workflows without extensive coding.

  • Ai Studio - a development environment for creating, configuring, and deploying these agents, enabling users to build, manage, and extend them, sometimes by linking multiple agents into complex workflows.

  • Zapier / Make — Workflow automation tools connecting existing SaaS apps. Visual, non-technical.

  • n8n — Open-source automation with custom code blocks and self-hosted control. Great for low-code tinkerers.

  • Replit — AI app development from idea to working prototype. Low-code, but requires some comfort reading code (currently in beta).

Actionable Tips for Your First Build

  1. Start with an Atomic Problem: Don’t try to build the whole travel agent at once. Build one piece: an agent that checks if a restaurant is open and emails you the address. That then feeds into the next agent, and the next. It minimizes surface area for errors.

  2. Make the Logic Visible: Use a “trace” or “log” step that shows the data moving through the workflow. You’ll instantly see if your timestamps are UTC or local.

  3. Assume the Docs Lag: If a step doesn’t work, skip the official docs and look for newer tutorials or community videos.

  4. Debug with an LLM: Copy cryptic error messages (and the related payloads) into Claude or GPT. Ask it to explain why the flow failed. Use the tool to understand the tool. Share screenshots to clarify when you’re lost in a UI.

  5. Build Trust Progressively: Don’t give your agent permission to book a $500 flight. Start with scheduling a 30-minute calendar block. Let it earn autonomy through reliability.

The Payoff

Building with Relay was messy. I broke things I didn’t understand.

I rewired integrations twice. I ran out of test credits. The docs lagged, and I was slow to catch up.

But now, when I design orchestration tools or agent experiences, I’m not speculating on what might fail. I’m remembering exactly how it failed for me. That’s the difference between empathy as a concept and empathy as a practice. By choosing to build the automation—not just the user interface—I earned the Ultimate Generalist Skill that so many early-2000s designers prized: the ability to design a full, messy, working system from the inside out.

Sometimes, the only way to practice is to build the thing yourself — bad JSON and all.

title: Comfort Shrinks Choice : Attention, Algorithms, and Agency
summary: What endless feeds and AI tools take from us, and how we can reclaim it.
body:
I opened TikTok for ten minutes. Suddenly, three hours were gone.

You’ve been there too—whether it’s YouTube, Instagram, Netflix, or whatever app grabs you. And it’s not just us. Our kids are growing up inside these loops, pulled into glowing rectangles that reward them for staying, not for leaving.

These systems are engineered for stickiness. Infinite scroll, autoplay, “For You” feeds, predictive text—they strip out friction and feed us tiny hits of dopamine. A 2024 study even found that skipping between videos to escape boredom intensifies boredom, lowering attention and meaning (PubMed). We think we’re escaping; the loop only deepens.

When was the last time you were bored? Really bored—sitting still with nothing to fill the gap. Researcher Sandi Mann calls boredom “the unnoticed driver of creativity.” Yet studies show digital media has made true boredom harder to come by (Nature Human Behaviour, 2024). That silence used to be fertile ground for imagination. Now it’s crowded out by algorithmically optimized distraction.

And that matters. Boredom isn’t wasted time—it’s the spark before possibility. Ursula K. Le Guin called imagination “the instrument of freedom.” Margaret Hamilton and her team of NASA engineers used it to code the guidance systems that carried humans to the moon. Those kinds of leaps don’t come from endlessly scrolling the familiar. They begin in the quiet stretch where the mind is free to wander, to play, to ask what if? When algorithms erase boredom, they erase the very soil where imagination takes root.

After all—Disney started with a mouse. Even the smallest ideas can take root and transform the world, but only if the soil of boredom isn’t paved over by constant distraction.

The tradeoff of convenience is choice. Algorithms don’t ask what will make us wiser or more creative—they ask what will keep us there. And when we coast, we confuse convenience with agency.

And this isn’t just about TikTok or Netflix. The same dynamics show up in how we use AI. Large language models are built on probability—they predict the most likely next word, just like your feed predicts the next clip. Left unchecked, they return the blandest, safest, most average answer.

But here’s the thing: choice is still ours. We don’t have to accept AI’s defaults. We can decide when to ask it for a counterpoint, when to press for surprise, and when to close the tab altogether. Awareness is the first step; control is the real work.

In fact, researchers are now measuring this. A 2025 benchmark called HumanAgencyBench tests how well AI assistants support human agency—whether they ask clarifying questions, resist manipulation, or reinforce user autonomy. Many models perform only moderately. It’s a reminder that “neutral” design isn’t neutral at all. The systems reflect choices made by their makers, and it’s on us to demand systems that protect our ability to choose, not just predict it.

This is where AI literacy comes in—not just knowing how to use tools, but understanding how they shape us. Studies now break literacy into four dimensions: knowing, applying, evaluating, and creating (ScienceDirect, 2024). True AI literacy means we stay aware of the cognitive shortcuts that make us trust the machine too quickly (authority bias), and resist letting efficiency replace judgment.

As some ethicists argue, algorithmic literacy isn’t just personal hygiene—it’s civic participation. Our ability to question, tweak, and resist defaults is what keeps the human in the loop.

How to Reclaim Choice

  • Break the loop, on purpose. If your feed looks predictable, don’t just scroll past—interrupt it. Click outside your pattern. Teach the system you won’t be reduced to past clicks.

  • Step outside the algorithm altogether. Log out. Go incognito. Borrow someone else’s account. Notice how the digital world looks different when it isn’t shaped by your data. Those contrasts reveal just how much you’re usually steered.

  • Use AI as a tool you steer, not a feed you swallow. Don’t settle for the most likely answer. Ask for what’s missing, what contradicts, what surprises. Direct the system instead of letting it direct you.

  • Reclaim the pause. Autoplay is designed to erase the moment of decision. Turn it off. Protect that silence between clips, songs, or episodes—it’s the gap where you get to choose.

  • Seek friction in a frictionless world. The best discoveries don’t always come “recommended for you.” Pick up a book, find a voice outside your algorithm, build a playlist by hand. Friction isn’t failure—it’s freedom.

  • Advocate for algorithmic choice. Right now, the dials exist, but they’re tuned for advertisers, not for us. Imagine if you could slide between diversity and similarity, depth and speed, delight and doom. Those settings don’t exist because it’s easier for companies to profit from passivity. If we want real choice, we have to demand it.

“The ultimate freedom is a free mind, and we need technology that’s on our team to help us live, feel, think and act freely.”
—Tristan Harris

Your Turn to Ask

  • If an algorithm is training on you, what exactly are you training it to value?

  • When was the last time you were truly bored—and what did that space open up for you?

  • Why do we accept opaque algorithms in our feeds, when we’d never accept a food label that hides the ingredients?

  • If you could rewrite your algorithm by default, which one would you change first?

Further Reading

  • Fast-forward to Boredom (PubMed, 2024)

  • People are increasingly bored in our digital age (Nature Human Behaviour, 2024)

  • From passive to active: Algorithm awareness and engagement (ScienceDirect, 2025)

  • HumanAgencyBench: Scalable Evaluation of Human Agency Support in AI Assistants (arXiv, 2025)

  • AI Literacy Framework: Knowing, Using, Evaluating, Creating (ScienceDirect, 2024)

title: I Let an AI Agent Plan My Summer Trip to Utah
summary: What worked, what didn’t, and why I’d absolutely do it again — with new lessons on trust and delegation.
body:
Inside tech, travel is the canonical demo for agents. Book the flights, reorder your day when it rains, suggest dinner nearby. It’s smooth on a slide deck, persuasive in a keynote.

But living it is different. This summer, I worked with an AI agent that I built to plan our family’s road trip through Utah’s national parks. Seven days, a rental SUV, three humans with very different thresholds for heat and adventure. What surprised me most wasn’t the itinerary itself, but how well the AI understood us and our needs.

I could share all the quirks that make traveling with my family unique — an almost-ten-year-old fascinated by geology and dinosaurs, a partner who wilts in desert heat, my ankle injury that rules out backcountry scrambles — and the agent suggested hikes, pie detours, and scenic stops that felt exactly right. It was personal, delightful, and in practice gave us the kind of vacation we actually wanted.

Where it fell down was in the details. Every event it added to the calendar came through in East Coast time instead of Mountain, which meant we technically had “sunset at 2pm.” Restaurants needed triple-checking since many were closed for summer holidays. Driving times were inconsistent.

Still, by putting it all into a shared calendar, we skipped the usual family friction: what should we do next, should we make a reservation, what time should we leave? The rhythm was there, and that made the trip feel lighter.

Why an Agent, Not Just a Chat

If you’ve used ChatGPT or another large language model (LLM), you know the pattern: you type a question, it gives an answer, maybe you refine with another prompt. That’s a conversation thread. It remembers what you’ve said during that session, but it isn’t built to do things beyond text.

An agent is different. It’s not just one big model giving you answers; it’s a system you design with roles, workflows, and sometimes sub-agents. An agent can:

  • Remember and reuse information across tasks.

  • Pull in outside tools, like calendars or maps.

  • Follow a workflow you define (first find hikes, then check distances, then add them to the calendar).

In the last year, agentic systems have advanced dramatically. What used to require complex Python workflows is now possible with no-code orchestration and memory layers built directly into platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, and CrewAI. Agents are learning to reason, recall, and collaborate — traits that used to define humans, not software.

When I built my Utah travel planner, I didn’t want a string of answers I had to copy-paste into notes. I wanted something that could hold onto my family’s needs, structure the days, and create a plan we could use together. That’s why I built an agent — so the experience was more like working with an assistant who drafts and organizes, rather than a chatbot who forgets between turns.

Building the Agent Around My Family

When I say I “built an agent,” I don’t mean I coded a complex system from scratch. I mean I treated the planning like a design problem: define the roles, set the workflow, add constraints — and then give the agent enough autonomy to act inside those guardrails.

Here’s what mine handled:

  • Finding trails that matched our abilities and interests, pulling directly from AllTrails.

  • Owning my calendar, adding and adapting key times like auto adding flights, Airbnb check-ins, and driving windows — it connected anything with a reservation link within our travel time frame so I didn’t have to hunt through my inbox.

  • Creating a custom map of our route, so we always had a shared visual anchor.

  • Surfacing restaurants for reservations — not booking yet, but narrowing the field and linking out so I could confirm.

  • Building a personalized booklet with trivia, wildlife notes, and fun facts we printed out for the car — which turned drive time into something more like a time machine, moving us up through the Grand Staircase in conversation instead of scrolling our phones.

What impressed me most was how natural multi-turn reasoning felt — the agent could take a half-formed idea (“a drive that ends in pie”) and transform it into a mapped sequence of stops. That’s a small taste of where things are headed: context-rich, memory-enabled systems that feel less like automation and more like collaboration.

It wasn’t perfect — the calendar did’nt take into account east to central timezones meaning my calendar thought sunset happened at 2pm, and several restaurants were closed for vacation despite being marked open — but the scaffolding was there. And because it held so much of the routine work, we were freed up to notice the real trip: the topography, the geology, the pie detours, the awe of those cliffs.

That’s the difference between a chat thread and an agent. A thread gives you answers you have to assemble. An agent takes on responsibility — planning, organizing, presenting — and gives you a system you can actually live inside.

I was actually able to relax, and enjoy the trip rather than spend my time away from devices, on them.

Do’s and Don’ts learnings

  • Do design your agent with your real constraints in mind. The more I baked in our limits and quirks — kid-friendly hikes, heat sensitivity, my ankle injury — the better it tailored the plan.

  • Do use your agent for scaffolding. One big hike plus smaller optional adventures per day turned out to be the perfect cadence.

  • Do let it surprise you with detours. Walmart runs and Capitol Reef pie stops were as memorable as the national park hikes.

  • Don’t trust calendar entries without verifying time zones. My agent happily booked us “sunset walks at 2pm in July”

  • Don’t assume restaurants will be open just because the agent says so. Vacation closures tripped us up more than once.

  • Don’t hand over judgment. Scrambles in 100-degree heat with a nine-year-old? No prompt can make that a good idea.

Working with an agent I built was like working with a junior teammate. It could draft the scaffolding, but I had to steer the decisions.

How You Can Build Your Own Travel Agent: A Starter Guide

You don’t need to be an engineer to try this. Most modern platforms — including ChatGPT’s agent builder — let you set up lightweight agents without writing code. What matters most is how clearly you define the problem and the workflow.

Here’s a simple recipe to try:

  1. Define the role. “You are my travel planning agent.”

  2. Set the task. “Plan a five-day family trip with one moderate hike per day and scenic drives in the afternoons.”

  3. List inputs. “Two adults, one child, heat-sensitive, prefer kid-friendly restaurants.”

  4. Add constraints. “No hikes over 15 miles. Confirm local time zones. Suggest only restaurants that will be open.”

  5. Choose outputs. “Deliver a day-by-day itinerary, add events to my calendar, and create trivia questions we can print for the car.”

  6. Work in turns. Start with the draft itinerary. Then ask it to cross-check restaurants. Then format into calendar events. Iteration is where the value happens.

  7. Stay in the loop. Treat the agent like a junior assistant. Let it draft and organize — but review before you approve or book.

Once you get the hang of it, you can expand — chaining across maps, calendars, and even reservation systems using platforms built for orchestration.

Benefits and Drawbacks

Working with an agent wasn’t magic, but it wasn’t hype either. The benefits were real:

  • Personalization. The agent actually understood us — one big hike per day, no scrambles, heat sensitivity, kid-friendly trivia. It didn’t hand me a generic “Top 10 Utah Attractions” list, it built something shaped to our family.

  • Structure without friction. Having everything in one shared calendar cut down on the “what should we do next?” debates. It created a rhythm that matched our energy.

  • Delightful extras. The trivia and wildlife notes transformed car rides into conversations. Instead of staring at screens, we were looking out the window, piecing together geology, laughing about dinosaurs, and imagining ourselves inside the landscape.

But the drawbacks showed where today’s agents still fall short:

  • Driving estimates. Travel times weren’t always accurate, which matters in the desert where the next stop could be hours away.

  • Trust. I wasn’t ready to let the agent book anything independently or touch a credit card. That meant I was still very hands-on, approving every reservation and double-checking every detail.

The benefits outweighed the drawbacks — enough that I’d absolutely do it again — but the cracks showed me what needs to come next.

Would I Use Agents Again?

Absolutely — and more so. My Utah trip wasn’t flawless, but it convinced me that the agent model is the right one. Next time, though, I’d set mine up differently, drawing from what I’ve learned since about multi-turn and multi-agent systems.

The next wave of agents is already pushing beyond static workflows. Gemini’s multimodal reasoning, OpenAI’s memory API, and frameworks like LangChain and CrewAI are enabling persistent agents that can learn from your preferences over time. That’s where the magic — and the responsibility — really begins for designers.

Here’s what I’d add:

  • Break tasks into sub-agents. Instead of one overworked agent juggling everything, I’d use specialized ones: a time-zone agent to sanity-check calendars, a restaurant agent pulling live data, a logistics agent recalculating drive times. Orchestration beats overload.

  • Design multi-turn prompts. In Utah, I gave my agent long, single-shot instructions. Next time I’d use a multi-turn workflow: first generate a draft plan, then cross-check it, then format it into my calendar. Prompt chaining is more reliable than dumping it all in at once.

  • Give the agent memory. The Utah agent could plan a week, but it didn’t remember my edits. Next time, I’d add a memory layer so it learns over time: “No scrambles,” “Prefer one big hike + downtime,” “Always check closures.”

  • Add guardrails. Just because an agent can suggest something doesn’t mean it should. Guardrails are what keep “sunset at 2pm” out of my calendar — and what could eventually make me comfortable enough to hand over booking power.

  • Earn my trust with transparency. Right now, I wouldn’t let an agent book independently or touch my credit card. The path forward is clear communication: what it’s doing, why it’s doing it, what it costs. Trust isn’t a feature; it’s the foundation.

  • Orchestrate across systems. Most of my Utah planning still required bouncing between ChatGPT, Gemini, maps, and calendars. With platforms like Relay.app, CrewAI, or Devin AI, the agent itself can chain across calendars, maps, and reservations without me as the middleman. That’s the shift from “AI as conversation” to “AI as co-worker.”

Would I trust an agent to plan another trip? Absolutely — because the foundation is already there. The personalization, the rhythm, the trivia that turned our drives into a time machine moving us up through the Grand Staircase — that part worked beautifully.

The difference next time will be giving my agent the autonomy, memory, and transparency it needs to grow from a helpful intern into a trusted travel companion.

Where to Go Next

If you want to try building your own agent, here are excellent starting points:

  • OpenAI’s documentation on agents — a clear overview of how to structure roles, tools, and memory.

  • LangChain agent guides — practical examples of multi-step and multi-turn workflows.

  • CrewAI — an open-source framework for orchestrating multiple specialized agents.

  • Relay.app — a no-code tool for chaining agents with calendars, email, and maps.

  • Voiceflow — for designing agent conversations visually.

  • Gemini — not just a chatbot, but a reasoning model that can serve as one of the specialized agents in your workflow.

We’re moving toward an ecosystem where every digital experience — from travel to healthcare to productivity — will have agentic underpinnings. For UX designers, the question isn’t whether to design for agents, but how to design with them.

Would I let an AI agent plan my next trip? Absolutely. Because the work of building and guiding it is part of the reward — and the payoff is a journey that feels more connected, more intentional, and more alive.

title: "This Just Sounds Like AI"
summary: Practical advice on why context and coaching—not code—make the difference between AI that’s just noise and AI that’s genuinely useful.
body:
I keep hearing people say, “this just sounds like AI” or “my [Insert your favorite LLM here] knows me so well, but it doesn’t sound like me.” That frustration isn’t a failure of the models. It’s how we’re working with them.

Over the past few months I’ve noticed a wave of frameworks trying to answer that problem. Stanford professor Jeremy Utley’s talk, Practical Guide to 10x Your AI Productivity, introduced the idea of “context engineering” and coaching machines like teammates. Creators like Tina Huang are publishing fast-moving guides on essential AI skills. Wharton researchers describe prompting as “complicated and contingent.” Microsoft is publishing design principles for autonomous agents. The World Economic Forum is already looking ahead to the UX challenges of multi-agent systems.

The common thread? They’re all circling the same idea: the difference between AI that spits out results and AI that proves useful isn’t syntax. It’s how we coach, frame, and direct it.

This is a moving target, but here is how I’m thinking and approaching this area.

From Prompts to Briefs

A throwaway prompt will get you a throwaway result. Ask an AI “write me a PRD” and you’ll get filler. Ask it “draft a PRD for a payments flow for Gen Z freelancers, tone casual, include edge cases and a risk section” and suddenly the response looks usable.

That’s not an AI trick. That’s a design brief. Utley calls it “context engineering,” and a recent Prompt Report catalogued more than 50 variations on the theme—few-shot, chain-of-thought, self-consistency—each useful in different contexts. But as Wharton researchers remind us, prompt design is complicated and contingent. Tiny changes in phrasing can flip a model’s behavior in surprising ways.

In other words, prompting isn’t a one-and-done trick. It’s an iterative design process in its own right.

When AI Asks the Questions

One of Utley’s most practical moves was “reverse prompting”: letting the AI ask you clarifiers instead of making shaky assumptions. It’s like a junior teammate pausing to ask, “who’s the audience for this?” before they start.

The Reflexive Prompt Engineering framework goes further—arguing that prompts should embed ethics, fairness, and accountability from the start. A clarifying AI isn’t just more accurate; it’s safer.

Shifting the posture from vending machine to curious intern is what makes AI feel less frustrating—and more collaborative.

Show Your Work

Another technique: chain-of-thought reasoning. Ask the AI not just for the answer, but to explain step by step how it got there. The process is often messy, sometimes wrong—but it gives you a window into its logic.

It feels like being in design critique with a new hire. You don’t care if they’re perfectly right; you care if you can follow the thinking. With AI, the same rule applies: don’t just accept the output, interrogate the path.

Flight Simulators for Tough Moments

One of Utley’s ideas is a “flight simulator” for hard conversations: three AI windows, one profiling the stakeholder, another roleplaying them, a third giving feedback on your approach.

It’s not about replacing the conversation. It’s about lowering the stakes so you can practice. Like rehearsing a pitch before a board meeting, or running through objections before talking to a skeptical partner. The AI isn’t the star—it’s the sparring partner.

Agents With Agency

The biggest shift is the rise of AI agents—systems that don’t just respond, but act. They can plan, fetch tools, even anticipate needs. Which sounds powerful… until one starts chiming in with help you didn’t ask for.

We’ve been here before: Slack bots that flood channels, or calendar nudges that arrive a beat too late. With agents, the stakes are higher. They only become teammates when they earn trust. And sometimes the smartest design choice is silence.

Microsoft’s UX Design for Agents stresses that autonomy without transparency erodes trust. Aubergine’s Designing for AI Agents argues the job isn’t just interface design anymore—it’s orchestration and oversight: when to let an agent act, when to rein it in, and when to hand control back. And the World Economic Forum is already warning that the challenge won’t be one agent, but many: multi-agent systems where latency, role ambiguity, and even agent-to-agent trust create a new layer of UX problems.

Directing the Vibe

“Vibe coding” is getting airtime—describe what you want, and AI spits out code. But the vibe doesn’t live in the code. It lives in the choices that come before.

The tiny ferrets carry dangerous code framework (Thinking, Frameworks, Checkpoints, Debugging, Context) is essentially a reminder that the real leverage is in vision, taste, and guardrails. That’s the work of directing the vibe, not typing the syntax.

Think of Airbnb’s design language—it’s not just pixels, it’s how the whole thing feels. That won’t come from a compiler.

Overwhelmed? Me too…

None of this feels like the predictable march of sprints. It feels like chaotic surges—waves of new capability, followed by troughs where teams scramble to apply it responsibly.

Our job isn’t to ride every wave. It’s to direct them. To translate raw capability into products that solve problems without drowning users in noise. That takes a different kind of literacy—not syntax, but coaching. Not coding, but context.

The so-called soft skills—framing, clarity, facilitation—are proving to be the hardest edge we have. They’re what makes the difference between AI that spits out results and AI that actually proves useful.
